title: From LAL-D to MASLD: Insights into the role of LAL and Kupffer cells in liver inflammation and lipid metabolism
projectDescription: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a prevalent liver pathology worldwide, closely associated with obesity and metabolic disorders. Increasing evidence suggests that macrophages play a crucial role in the development of MASLD. Several human studies have shown an inverse correlation between circulating lysosomal acid lipase (LAL) activity and MASLD. LAL is the sole enzyme known to degrade cholesteryl esters (CE) and triacylglycerols in lysosomes. Consequently, these substrates accumulate when their enzymatic degradation is impaired due to LAL deficiency (LAL-D). This study aimed to investigate the role of hepatic LAL activity and liver-resident macrophages (i.e., Kupffer cells (KC)) in MASLD. To this end, we analyzed lipid metabolism in hepatocyte-specific (hep)Lal-/- mice and depleted KC with clodronate treatment. When fed a high-fat/high-cholesterol diet (HF/HCD), hepLal-/- mice exhibited CE accumulation and an increased number of macrophages in the liver without significantly affecting liver injury. KC were depleted upon clodronate administration, whereas infiltrating/proliferating CD68-expressing macrophages were less affected. This led to exacerbated hepatic CE accumulation and dyslipidemia, as evidenced by increased LDL-cholesterol concentrations. The results suggest that hepatic LAL-D in HF/HCD-fed mice leads to macrophage infiltration into the liver, and KC depletion further aggravates hepatic CE levels and dyslipidemia, a finding also supported by our proteomics analysis.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Thirty milligrams of pulverized, homogenized liver tissue were lysed using 1.4-mm ceramic beads (OMNI International, Inc., Kennesaw, GA) in a 50 mM HEPES buffer (pH 8.5) containing 5% sodium deoxycholate (SDC), supplemented with 1x cOmplete™ EDTA-free Protease Inhibitor Cocktail and PhosSTOP phosphatase inhibitors (Sigma–Aldrich, St. Louis, MO). The samples were then diluted to a final concentration of 2.5% SDC in 50 mM HEPES (pH 8.5) and subjected to sonication for 4 cycles of 30 seconds each at 60% amplitude. To denature the proteins, the samples were heated to 99 °C and shaken at 700 rpm for 5 minutes. After centrifugation at 20,000 × g for 20 minutes, the infranatant was transferred to a new low-binding tube, and protein concentration was measured using the Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA. Twenty mikrograms of protein were reduced with 10 mM DTT and alkylated with 20 mM iodoacetamide. Protein digestion was performed overnight at 37 °C using LysC (0.04 activity units per mg of protein) and trypsin (5%). The following day, an additional 1% trypsin was added, and the samples were incubated for 2 hours at 37 °C. Half of the digested proteins were transferred to a new tube, and SDC was precipitated with 2% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA). After centrifugation at 20,000 × g for 5 minutes, the supernatant was purified using C18 stage tips (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were eluted from the C18 tips with 65% acetonitrile in 0.1% TFA, vacuum-dried, and resuspended in 50 µL of 0.1% formic acid, followed by shaking at 2,500 rpm for 15 minutes. Peptide concentrations were determined using the NanoPhotometer N60 (IMPLEN, Munich, Germany), and 200 ng of peptides were loaded onto EvoTips (Evosep, Odense, Denmark) according to the manufacturer's instructions.  The peptides were separated using the "30 samples per day" method on a 15-cm EV1106 Endurance Column packed with 150 μM C18 beads (1.9 μm) (Evosep) on an Evosep ONE HPLC system connected to a timsTOF Pro 2 mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics, Bremen, Germany). The mass spectrometer operated in dia-PASEF mode with a CaptiveSpray ionization source, collecting MS data between 100 and 1,700 m/z. TIMS settings were configured with a 1/K0 range from 0.6 to 1.6 Vs/cm², a ramp time of 100 ms, and an accumulation time of 100 ms. Ion mobility calibration was performed using 622.0290, 922.0098, and 1221.9906 Tuning Mix ES-TOF standards. Dia-PASEF cycles lasted 1.7 s, with 26 mass steps per cycle, spanning a 1/K0 range of 0.66 to 1.4 Vs/cm².
dataProcessingProtocol: Protein quantification was carried out using DIA-NN (v1.9) by searching the raw data against the reviewed Mouse Uniprot FASTA file, which was downloaded on July 1, 2024. The following parameters were applied for precursor ion generation: FASTA digestion for library-free search and library generation; deep learning-based prediction of spectra, retention time, and ion mobility; and trypsin digestion with allowance for up to 2 missed cleavages. Fixed modifications included N-terminal methionine excision and carbamidomethylation of cysteine, while a maximum of 2 variable modifications were allowed, including methionine oxidation and N-terminal acetylation. The peptide length was restricted to a range of 7–30 amino acids, with a precursor charge range of 1–4 and a precursor m/z range of 300–1800. Fragment ion m/z range was set between 200–1800. The precursor false discovery rate (FDR) was maintained at 1%, with mass accuracy and MS1 accuracy set to 15 ppm and 20 ppm, respectively. Additional features such as peptidoform quantification, match between runs, heuristic protein inference, and exclusion of shared spectra were enabled. Protein inference was performed at the gene level, while all other parameters were kept at their default settings.
